title: Finding past invoices
body:
Every invoice Meridian generates is kept in your workspace's billing history for as long as the account is active, not just the current billing period.

Open Settings → Billing → Invoices to see the full list, ordered by billing date with the most recent at the top. The billing tab's default view only surfaces the current month's invoice on the summary card; the invoices table below it holds every prior one.

Each row links to a PDF you can download or forward for expense reporting. If a specific month is missing from the list, the plan may not have generated a paid invoice for it — for example, a month fully covered by a credit produces no invoice.

title: Switching between monthly and annual billing
body:
Workspaces on a monthly plan can move to annual billing at any time from Settings → Billing → Plan.

Switching to annual takes effect immediately: the workspace is charged the annual rate on confirmation, prorated against any monthly charge already paid for the current period, and the renewal date resets to one year from the switch. It does not wait for the current monthly cycle to finish.

Switching back from annual to monthly is different — the annual discount was paid for a fixed term, so a downgrade to monthly billing takes effect at the end of the current annual term rather than immediately.

title: Correcting billing details on invoices
body:
A workspace's legal name, billing address and tax ID are set in Settings → Billing → Company details and are pulled onto every invoice generated after the change.

Meridian does not reissue invoices that have already been generated — a correction applies to invoices from that point forward only. This is a bookkeeping constraint on both sides: a reissued invoice with a different legal entity on it can complicate a customer's own accounting for a period already closed.

Customers who need a corrected copy of a past invoice for their own records, rather than a reissue, can request one through support.

title: Changing who receives invoice emails
body:
By default, invoice emails go to the workspace's billing contact, which is usually whoever set up billing originally.

To send invoices to a different address — a shared finance inbox, for example — open Settings → Billing → Recipients and add or replace the billing contact email. Multiple recipients can be added, so a shared inbox can be added alongside rather than instead of an individual's address.

The change applies to the next invoice generated after it is saved; it does not resend past invoices to the new address.

title: Payment methods Meridian accepts
body:
Meridian bills by card by default on both monthly and annual plans.

Annual contracts can also be paid by bank transfer against an invoice, which is arranged through support before the contract starts rather than self-served from the billing settings — bank transfer requires setting the account up for invoiced billing rather than automatic card charges.

Monthly plans are card-only; a workspace wanting bank transfer needs to be on an annual term first.

title: Reading an itemised invoice
body:
Every invoice breaks its total down into three kinds of line item: the seat charge for the billing period, any add-ons enabled on the plan, and usage overages for anything metered beyond the plan's included allowance.

Open the invoice from Settings → Billing → Invoices and expand a line item to see its own breakdown — a seat charge, for example, itemises how many seats were billed and at what per-seat rate, and an overage line shows the metered quantity against the plan's included limit.

The downloadable PDF includes the same breakdown, so it can be attached to an internal budget review without needing to also share dashboard access.

title: When invoices are generated
body:
A monthly plan is invoiced on the same day of the month as the workspace's original billing date — the date the subscription started or last renewed.

That date is shown in Settings → Billing → Plan next to “Next invoice”, and it does not shift month to month even though months have different lengths; a billing date of the 31st bills on the last day of a shorter month.

Because the card charge happens on that date, replacing a card a day or two beforehand is enough for the new card to be used for the upcoming invoice.

title: Troubleshooting an SSO redirect loop
body:
A sign-in that returns to the login page immediately after the identity provider approves it is almost always a redirect URL mismatch rather than a credentials problem.

Meridian's SSO integration expects the identity provider's assertion to be posted back to a specific callback URL, shown in Settings → Security → SSO → Configuration. That URL must match, character for character, what is entered as the reply URL or redirect URI on the identity provider's side — a trailing slash or an http/https mismatch is enough to cause the loop.

1. Open the SSO configuration page and copy the callback URL exactly.
2. Compare it against the reply URL configured at the identity provider.
3. Re-save the identity provider's application if any difference is found, since some providers cache the old value until it is re-saved.

title: Rolling out SSO without locking staff out
body:
Enabling SSO does not immediately disable password sign-in for existing staff. Both methods coexist until an admin separately turns password sign-in off, in Settings → Security → SSO → Require SSO.

This is deliberate: a rollout usually needs a period where some staff have been provisioned through the identity provider and others have not yet, and forcing SSO before everyone is provisioned would lock the unprovisioned staff out entirely.

Once every staff member has confirmed they can sign in through SSO, enabling “Require SSO” turns off password sign-in for the whole workspace in one step.

title: Why a staff member might not see SSO on sign-in
body:
The SSO sign-in option only appears for an email domain the workspace has configured for SSO, and only once the identity provider sync has actually created that person's account.

A new hire who does not see it may be signing in before the next scheduled sync has run, or their account may not yet exist on the identity provider's side of the integration — Meridian never creates accounts on its own for an SSO-enabled domain, only through the sync.

An admin can check whether the account exists from Settings → People, where an SSO-provisioned account is marked with the identity provider it came from; its absence means the sync has not created it yet.

title: Setting up two-factor authentication
body:
Two-factor authentication is enabled per account from Settings → Security → Two-factor authentication, and does not require an admin to turn anything on workspace-wide first.

1. Open Settings → Security → Two-factor authentication and select “Enable”.
2. Scan the QR code with an authenticator app.
3. Enter the six-digit code the app generates to confirm enrolment.
4. Save the recovery codes shown afterwards somewhere safe — they are the only way back in if the device is lost.

Once enabled, sign-in asks for a code from the app after the password, on every new session.

title: Re-enrolling two-factor authentication after losing access to the app
body:
An authenticator app reinstalled after a phone upgrade starts generating new codes that no longer match what Meridian has on file, because the original enrolment's secret was tied to the old install.

From Settings → Security → Two-factor authentication, choose “Reset” and re-enrol the same way as a first-time setup — scanning a new QR code and confirming with a fresh six-digit code. A saved recovery code from the original enrolment can also be used to sign in and reset from there if the settings page itself is not reachable without a working code.

Re-enrolling invalidates the old QR code entirely; only the newly scanned one will generate valid codes afterward.

title: Identity providers Meridian supports for SSO
body:
Meridian's SSO integration supports any identity provider that speaks SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect, which covers the major providers in common use.

A workspace configures exactly one identity provider at a time, tied to the email domains it covers in Settings → Security → SSO → Domains. Consolidating two teams that came from different providers onto one workspace means picking one provider as the SSO source of truth and migrating the other team's accounts to it, rather than running both providers against the same workspace at once.

Support can advise on migration order for a specific pair of providers, since the identity provider side of that move is usually the slower half.

title: Exporting more than ten thousand records
body:
A single export from the dashboard is capped at ten thousand rows, which keeps the download generating in the browser rather than timing out on very large workspaces.

For a report larger than that, narrow the export with a date range or filter so each export stays under the cap, and run it more than once to cover the full period — for example, one export per month rather than one for the whole quarter.

Workspaces that regularly need a full, uncapped history should use the scheduled export to cloud storage instead, which is not subject to the ten-thousand-row browser cap.

title: Column headers the contact importer expects
body:
The contact importer reads a CSV file and matches columns by header name, not by position, so the columns can be in any order as long as the headers match.

Required headers are `email`, `name` and `company`; optional headers include `phone`, `title` and any custom field already defined on the workspace, matched by the custom field's own name. A header the importer does not recognise is ignored rather than rejected, so an extra column from a spreadsheet export will not block the import.

Downloading the sample template from the import screen is the fastest way to get the exact header spelling the importer expects.

title: Why an import might reject rows with no visible error
body:
An import that succeeds for some rows and silently drops others is usually failing per-row validation that is not surfaced on the main import screen — a missing required field, a malformed email, or a duplicate that the importer treats as a skip rather than a failure.

After an import finishes, open Settings → Data → Import history and select the run: it lists a per-row result, including a reason for every row that did not import. This detail is not shown during the import itself, only afterward in the history.

Fixing the flagged rows and re-running the import against just those rows, rather than the whole file, avoids re-processing the rows that already succeeded.

title: Scheduling a recurring export
body:
Recurring exports are configured from Settings → Data → Scheduled exports, separately from the one-off export button on the dashboard.

1. Choose what to export and on what recurrence — daily, weekly or monthly.
2. Connect a cloud storage destination; Meridian supports the major providers via an OAuth connection made once per destination.
3. Save the schedule.

Each run lands as a new file in the connected destination rather than overwriting the previous one, and the scheduled exports screen shows the history of runs along with whether each one succeeded.

title: What a standard export includes
body:
A standard export from the dashboard includes every record in the current view, including archived and closed ones, unless a filter on the export screen narrows it to a status.

The active queue view that most people work from by default hides closed records, but the export screen's own filter is independent of whatever view was open when the export was started — it is worth checking the export screen's filter directly rather than assuming it inherited the dashboard's current filter.

To confirm exactly what was included, the row count shown before starting the export can be compared against the workspace's total record count including archives, found in Settings → Data → Overview.

title: Avoiding duplicates when re-importing a corrected file
body:
The importer matches existing records by email for contacts, or by the record's own unique identifier where one is provided in the file, and updates a match in place rather than creating a second copy.

A row that succeeded on the first import and is present again, unchanged, in a corrected file will be recognised as the same record and updated rather than duplicated — as long as the matching field itself was not the thing that needed correcting.

If the correction was to the email address or identifier used for matching, the importer has no way to recognise it as the same row, and the safest approach is to remove the already-succeeded rows from the corrected file before re-running it.

title: Choosing an export format
body:
Exports are offered in CSV, and in a spreadsheet-native format for the two most common spreadsheet tools, selectable from a dropdown on the export screen.

CSV is the safest default for compatibility with any tool, including ones not offered as a native option, but loses column types — dates and numbers come through as plain text and need reformatting after import. The native formats preserve column types and formulas are not included since exports are values only.

For a one-off download destined for a specific tool, picking that tool's native format avoids a manual reformatting step CSV would otherwise require.

title: What counts against the API rate limit
body:
The documented rate limit is per API key, not per workspace, and it is a rolling window rather than a fixed per-minute bucket — requests from the last sixty seconds are counted continuously, not reset at the top of each minute.

A key well under the per-minute figure can still receive `429` responses if requests arrive in a burst rather than spread evenly, because the rolling window counts the burst as concentrated in a shorter span than a minute.

Every response carries `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers showing the exact count and window against that key, which is the reliable way to see what is actually being counted rather than inferring it from the documented headline figure.

title: Checking webhook delivery status
body:
A webhook endpoint that stops receiving events with nothing surfaced in the receiving system's own logs usually means the deliveries are failing before they reach that system — a TLS certificate that expired, a firewall change, or the endpoint returning a non-2xx status that never gets logged as an error locally.

Settings → Developer → Webhooks → Delivery log shows every attempt Meridian made against the endpoint, including the HTTP status returned and the response body, independent of whatever the receiving system logged on its own end.

Deliveries that fail are retried on a backoff schedule for a limited window; past that window a failed delivery is not retried automatically and the event would need to be replayed manually from the delivery log.

title: Rotating an API key
body:
Generating a new API key from Settings → Developer → API keys does not automatically revoke the old one — both keys are valid at the same time until the old one is explicitly revoked.

This overlap window exists so a key can be rotated without a moment of downtime: deploy the new key to whatever uses the old one, confirm it works, and only then revoke the old key from the same screen.

The delivery log and request logs are keyed by which API key made each call, so it is possible to confirm nothing is still using the old key before revoking it.

title: Webhook payload size and batching large records
body:
A webhook payload is capped at a fixed size, and a record whose full content would exceed it is delivered as a reference — an id and a `truncated: true` flag — rather than a truncated version of the content itself, so a consuming system should treat that flag as a signal to fetch the full record via the API rather than trust a partial payload.

For records that are frequently large, subscribing to the `.changed` event and fetching the current record by id, instead of relying on the webhook's own payload to carry the full content, avoids the size cap entirely.

Batching many changes into fewer webhook calls is not configurable — each change is delivered as its own event — so a batching strategy belongs on the receiving side, buffering fetched records rather than buffering webhook deliveries.

title: Sending a test webhook event
body:
Settings → Developer → Webhooks → Send test event fires a realistic sample payload at a configured endpoint on demand, without needing to create or change a real record to trigger it.

The test event uses the same schema and headers as a live delivery, including the signing header a receiving handler should verify, so a handler that passes the test event will handle a real one the same way.

The delivery log records test events alongside real ones, marked as test deliveries, which is useful for confirming the endpoint responded with a 2xx before wiring it to production traffic.

title: Paginating through the full API response
body:
List endpoints return one page of results at a time, with a `next_cursor` field in the response when more results exist — a response with no `next_cursor` is the last page, but a response that has not checked for one at all will silently stop at the first page.

An integration that reads only the first page will appear to work correctly for a small workspace and then quietly miss records once the result set grows past a single page, which is why the pagination cursor should be followed as a matter of course rather than added later once it becomes visibly wrong.

The API reference's pagination section shows the loop pattern — following `next_cursor` until it is absent — that every list endpoint expects a client to implement.

title: Which API endpoints are considered stable
body:
Every endpoint in the API reference is marked with a stability tag — `stable`, `beta` or `experimental` — shown next to its heading, and only `stable` endpoints carry the deprecation-notice commitment described in the API changelog policy.

A `beta` endpoint can change shape without the same advance notice a `stable` one gets, and an `experimental` endpoint can be removed outright. The changelog itself is the record of what actually changed and when, and is the place to check before relying on a beta endpoint's current shape for a production integration.

Subscribing to the changelog's feed surfaces a stability change or deprecation notice before it takes effect, rather than after an integration breaks.

title: Seat limits by plan
body:
Every plan tier has a maximum number of seats included, shown in Settings → Billing → Plan alongside how many are currently used. An invite that is blocked with no seats available means the workspace has reached that tier's limit.

Raising the limit means either adding seats within the current tier, if the plan allows purchasing additional seats beyond the included count, or upgrading to a tier with a higher included limit — Settings → Billing → Plan shows which option applies to the current plan.

Both changes take effect immediately once confirmed; the blocked invite can be resent right after.

title: Reassigning a seat without paying for two at once
body:
Removing a person from Settings → People frees their seat immediately, and inviting a new person into that freed seat does not add a new seat to the count as long as it happens within the same billing cycle — the seat count that matters for billing is the highest number of seats occupied at any point in the cycle, not the number of people who passed through it.

Removing the departed employee before inviting the new hire, rather than inviting first, keeps the occupied count from momentarily exceeding the paid seat count and triggering an overage charge for that cycle.

The next invoice bills the seat count as of the invoice date, so a same-cycle reassignment shows as one seat, not two.

title: Comparing plan tiers before upgrading
body:
Settings → Billing → Plan includes a full feature comparison across every tier, not just the seat limits — each tier's included seats, integrations, retention window and support level are shown side by side.

Nothing about existing data or configuration changes automatically as part of comparing tiers; the comparison page does not commit to anything until an upgrade is explicitly confirmed, so it can be reviewed and shared internally before authorising the spend.

A workspace that upgrades to see the comparison more clearly can also downgrade back within a short window with no charge, if the upgrade turns out not to be needed yet.

title: What happens to data when downgrading a plan
body:
Downgrading a plan does not delete anything. Features and data tied to a higher tier are hidden rather than removed — a downgraded workspace stops being able to use the feature, but the underlying data is preserved and becomes visible again immediately if the workspace upgrades back.

The one exception is data subject to the plan's retention window: a lower tier with a shorter retention period will, over time, age out records older than that window the same way it would for a workspace that started on that tier, rather than deleting them at the moment of downgrade.

Settings → Billing → Plan lists exactly which features are tier-gated before confirming a downgrade, so what will become hidden is known in advance.

title: What changes for integrations during a plan migration
body:
Moving a workspace to a new plan does not interrupt existing API keys, webhooks or automation rules — they continue running through the migration with no reconfiguration required, since they are tied to the workspace rather than to a specific plan tier.

The one thing that can change is a tier-gated automation feature: if a rule uses a capability only available on the destination tier, it activates as soon as the migration completes; if it depends on a capability the destination tier does not include, the rule is paused rather than deleted, and reactivates automatically if the workspace ever returns to a tier that includes it.

Settings → Automation → Rules shows the status of every rule, including any that migration would pause, before the migration is confirmed.

title: Changing a seat's role
body:
A seat's role — agent, admin or observer — is changed from Settings → People without removing and re-adding the person, so nothing about their identity or history on the workspace is affected by the change.

Assignment history is attached to the person's account, not to their current role, so records previously assigned to someone moving to observer remain assigned to them and remain visible in that history; an observer role only changes what the person can do going forward, specifically that new work cannot be assigned to them and they cannot take actions requiring an agent or admin role.

The role change takes effect on save and does not require the person to sign out and back in.

title: Correcting how timestamps are displayed
body:
Timestamps are stored once, in UTC, and displayed converted to a timezone — but which timezone is used depends on two separate settings: the workspace default, in Settings → General, and each person's own account timezone, in their personal Settings → Profile.

An account with no personal timezone set falls back to the workspace default, which is why two people in different timezones can see the same record displayed several hours apart from each other and both be seeing it correctly according to their own setting.

Setting a personal timezone in Profile settings overrides the workspace default for that account only, without changing what anyone else sees.

title: Why a newly created record might not appear in search yet
body:
Search runs against an index that is updated shortly after a record is created or changed, rather than reading live from the same data the browse views use — browsing always reflects the current state, but search can lag it by a short interval under normal load.

A record that is visible when browsing directly but does not yet appear in search is almost always this indexing delay rather than a search problem with the query itself; it resolves on its own within a couple of minutes without any action needed.

If a record still does not appear in search after several minutes, that is no longer expected indexing lag and is worth reporting rather than waiting further.

title: Reducing notification email volume
body:
Notification email settings are per person, in Profile → Notifications, and are separate from the workspace-wide notification rules an admin controls — narrowing your own volume does not require an admin to change anything.

Each notification type can be turned off independently — assignment, mention, status change and digest emails are listed separately — so “only what's assigned to me” is achieved by leaving assignment notifications on and turning the others off, rather than an all-or-nothing toggle.

Changes take effect immediately and only affect the account that made them; nothing about what other people see is changed by narrowing your own notifications.

title: Restoring a deleted project
body:
A deleted project is held in a recoverable state for thirty days before it is permanently removed, and can be restored within that window from Settings → Data → Deleted items by an admin.

Restoring a project brings back everything that was attached to it at the time of deletion — its records, its configuration and its automation rules — exactly as they were, rather than as a blank project with the same name.

Past the thirty-day window, deletion is permanent and support has no way to recover it; the window exists specifically to cover this kind of accidental deletion, so acting within it is the only recovery path.

title: Renaming a workspace
body:
A workspace's display name, changed in Settings → General, is cosmetic only — it does not change the workspace's URL, its API base path, or the identifiers any existing integration or webhook already references.

Every integration continues to point at the same workspace by its underlying id, which the rename does not touch, so nothing needs to be reconfigured after a rename purely because of the name change itself.

The one place the old name may persist visibly is in email addresses or subdomains a workspace chose to set up separately at an earlier point, which are configured independently and are not automatically updated by a display name rename.

title: Setting up a custom domain
body:
A custom domain for the support portal is configured from Settings → General → Custom domain, which shows the exact DNS records to add once a domain name is entered.

Two records are required: a `CNAME` pointing the chosen subdomain at Meridian's portal address, and a `TXT` record used to verify ownership of the domain before the custom domain is activated. Both are added at whichever provider hosts the domain's DNS, outside of Meridian.

Verification runs automatically and can take up to the DNS provider's own propagation time to complete; the custom domain settings page shows a pending or verified status so there is no need to guess whether it has taken effect.

title: Checking whether a scheduled report is still running
body:
Settings → Reports → Scheduled shows every scheduled report and its run history, including the outcome of its most recent run — a report that stopped sending shows either a failed run with a reason, or shows as disabled if it was turned off.

A common cause of a report silently stopping is the recipient list: a report keeps running on schedule even after a recipient's email starts bouncing, but Meridian pauses delivery to a bouncing address after repeated failures without pausing the report for other recipients, which can look like the whole report stopped.

The run history distinguishes between the report not running at all and the report running but failing to deliver, which is the first thing to check before assuming the schedule itself broke.

title: Getting historical usage data
body:
Usage data for the current and prior billing period is available directly from Settings → Billing → Usage, exportable as CSV from that screen without needing to request anything.

Usage older than the two most recent billing periods is retained but not shown on that screen by default; it can still be pulled with a custom date range from the same export, as long as the range falls within the workspace's overall data retention window.

For an audit needing a specific quarter, exporting with that quarter's exact date range from the usage screen produces the same data a request to support would, without the wait.

title: What counts toward response-time metrics
body:
By default, the response-time metric on the dashboard counts every hour a ticket sits unanswered, including nights, weekends and holidays — it is a wall-clock measurement, not a business-hours one.

A business-hours version of the same metric is available by configuring business hours in Settings → Reporting → Business hours and switching the dashboard's metric to “business hours” mode, which excludes time outside the configured hours from the calculation entirely rather than just displaying it differently.

Both versions can be shown side by side on a custom dashboard, which is useful when a raw wall-clock number needs context before it goes into a report.

title: Building a custom report grouped by tag
body:
The default reports group by status, but Reports → Custom → New report lets any report be built around a different grouping, including tag, assignee or a custom field.

Selecting “Tag” as the group-by dimension on a new custom report produces one row per tag, with the same metrics — count, average resolution time and so on — that the default reports show per status. A ticket with more than one tag is counted once under each of its tags, since a ticket can genuinely belong to more than one grouping at once.

Custom reports can be saved and scheduled the same way built-in reports can, once the grouping and metrics are set the way they're wanted.

title: Sharing a dashboard without giving the recipient a login
body:
Any dashboard can be shared as a read-only public link from the dashboard's own Share menu, which does not require the recipient to have a Meridian account or sign in at all.

The shared link stays live and updates in real time along with the dashboard itself — it is not a snapshot — so a stakeholder revisiting the link later sees current data rather than what it showed when the link was created.

Sharing can be revoked at any time from the same Share menu, which immediately invalidates the link for anyone who still has it.

title: Accessing data older than the retention window
body:
The dashboard's default view shows data within the plan's retention window, but data older than that is not deleted at the retention boundary on most plans — it moves to cold storage rather than disappearing, and remains available on request.

Settings → Reporting → Extended history describes what extended range, if any, is included on the current plan, and how to request older data where it is not shown by default. Some higher plan tiers include a longer retention window directly on the dashboard with no request needed.

For data old enough to fall outside even extended retention, availability depends on how long ago the workspace was created, since nothing is retained from before the workspace existed.

title: Checking the status page for a known incident
body:
Meridian's status page lists every incident affecting the platform, including brief ones, with the exact start and end time and which components were affected — a widespread `503` response, even a short one, is the kind of event that appears there rather than going unrecorded.

A component-level breakdown on the status page distinguishes an incident affecting the API from one affecting only the dashboard or another part of the platform, which is useful for confirming whether a specific symptom matches a listed incident rather than being unrelated.

Subscribing to the status page's updates surfaces an incident as it is happening rather than only after checking the page after the fact.

title: Telling a platform-wide slowdown from a local one
body:
A brief period of slower page loads that resolves on its own is worth checking against the status page first — a platform-wide degradation, even a short one not severe enough to be called a full incident, is usually listed there with a start and end time.

If nothing appears on the status page for that window, the slowdown was more likely local — a browser extension, network conditions, or a large amount of data loading for that specific workspace — rather than something affecting other customers.

The status page's history goes back further than just current incidents, so a window from earlier in the day can still be checked after the fact.

title: Subscribing to incident notifications
body:
The status page has a Subscribe option offering email, SMS or a webhook, delivering a notification the moment an incident is opened, updated or resolved — before it necessarily reaches customers through other channels.

A webhook subscription is the fastest way to route incident updates into an existing on-call or alerting tool, since it delivers the same update in real time without needing anyone to check email.

Subscriptions can be scoped to specific components rather than the whole platform, which keeps a team from being paged for incidents in a part of the platform they don't depend on.

title: Post-incident summaries
body:
Every resolved incident on the status page gets a written summary once the investigation is complete, describing what happened, the affected window, and — where relevant — whether any data was affected and how.

The summary is added to the same incident entry that showed the live updates during the incident, rather than published separately, so the full history of an incident from open to resolved to summarised lives in one place.

Summaries for incidents that did not affect data usually still note that explicitly, since “no summary yet” and “confirmed no data was affected” read very differently to someone checking after the fact.

title: How uptime service credits are calculated
body:
Meridian's uptime commitment and the service credit schedule tied to it are part of the account's contract terms, which vary by plan tier — the exact percentage guaranteed and the credit schedule for missing it are documented in the order form or contract for that workspace rather than in the general help centre, since they can differ between customers.

Where a contract includes an uptime guarantee, a credit is generally calculated as a percentage of that billing period's charges, scaled to how far actual uptime fell short of the guarantee, and applied to a future invoice rather than refunded directly.

A customer checking whether a specific incident qualifies, and for how much, should reference their own contract's schedule and can ask support to confirm the incident's measured uptime impact against it.

title: How Meridian handles disputed or duplicate charges
body:
A charge a customer believes was made in error — including an apparent duplicate — is reviewed by the billing team rather than reversed automatically from the dashboard, because reversing a charge changes money that has already moved and needs to be verified against the account's actual billing record first, not just against how the invoice appears to the person reporting it.

A review starts once the account owner or an authorised billing contact raises it, and the billing team checks the payment processor's own record of what was charged against what Meridian's system believes it charged — a duplicate on the processor's side and a duplicate on Meridian's side are different failures with different fixes.

Reviews are handled case by case and typically resolve within a few business days, though a specific charge's outcome and timeline are not something a help-centre article can state in advance of the review itself.

title: How mid-cycle seat changes are billed and reviewed
body:
Seats cancelled partway through a billing cycle are not automatically prorated on Meridian's standard plans — the general policy is that a seat removed mid-cycle stops being billed starting the next cycle rather than being refunded for the remainder of the current one, though contract terms can vary this for some accounts.

When a customer believes they were billed incorrectly against that policy — for example, if seats were removed before the cycle started and still appear charged — the billing team reviews the account's actual seat history against what was invoiced, rather than the customer's recollection of when the change was made, since the two can genuinely differ.

This kind of review is handled case by case, and the account owner or billing contact should raise it with the specific seats and dates in question so it can be checked against the record.

title: Disputing a usage overage charge
body:
An overage charge is generated from metered usage recorded automatically during the billing period, and a customer who believes it does not reflect their actual usage can ask the billing team to review the underlying metered data against the charge.

The review compares the raw usage record — not just the total shown on the invoice — against the threshold that would trigger an overage, which can surface causes a customer would not see from the dashboard alone, such as a metering bug, a misconfigured integration generating unexpected usage, or usage that genuinely occurred but was not visible from the view the customer was checking.

Because this involves verifying account-specific data against a specific charge, it is handled case by case by a human reviewer rather than resolved from a general article, and the account owner or billing contact is the one who can raise it.

title: Currency and billing region corrections
body:
A workspace's billing currency follows its configured billing region, and a charge made against a stale or incorrect region setting is reviewed by the billing team once reported, since correcting it involves reconciling what was actually charged in the wrong currency against what should have been charged in the correct one.

The region setting itself can be corrected going forward by the account owner from billing settings, but a correction to a charge that has already been processed — since it involves money that has already moved between currencies — is not something the settings page reverses on its own.

Because the amount and exchange rate involved differ per account and per charge, this is reviewed case by case rather than handled by a fixed formula in a published article, and the account owner or billing contact should raise the specific invoice in question.

title: Charges after a cancellation
body:
Cancelling a subscription is meant to stop the next renewal charge, and a charge that lands anyway after a cancellation was submitted is treated as a billing discrepancy the billing team investigates directly, since it usually means either the cancellation did not fully process before the renewal ran, or the charge and the cancellation happened close enough together that their order matters.

The review checks the account's cancellation record against the exact timing of the charge, which is account-specific and not something a general article can determine, and confirms both what happened and what the account's ongoing renewal status now is.

This is handled case by case by a human reviewer, and the account owner or billing contact should raise it with the date the cancellation was submitted.

title: Renewal pricing questions
body:
An annual plan generally renews at the account's then-current list price unless a specific renewal price was contractually locked in at the time of the original quote — whether a locked price applies to a given account depends on the terms agreed when that account was set up, which is not something a general pricing article can state for every customer.

Where a customer believes their renewal did not reflect a price they were quoted, the billing team checks the account's own contract or order form against what was actually charged at renewal, since that is the record that determines what price should have applied.

This is reviewed case by case, and the account owner or billing contact should raise it referencing the original quote so it can be checked against the account's terms.

title: Reporting a suspected account compromise
body:
A login from an unfamiliar location followed by a change to sensitive account details — like the billing contact email — is exactly the pattern Meridian's security review process exists for, and it is handled by a human reviewer rather than resolved automatically from any settings page.

Reporting it starts with the account owner or an admin contacting support directly rather than attempting to undo the change themselves first, since a reviewer needs to see the account's actual activity and change history before anything is reversed, and undoing a change before it is reviewed can sometimes remove evidence of what happened.

Once reported, a reviewer verifies the identity of who is reporting it, examines the account's sign-in and change history, and determines what needs to be locked down or reversed — this varies enough by account that it is not something a general article can walk through step by step.

title: Reporting an unrecognised or compromised API key
body:
An API key active on a workspace that nobody recognises generating it is treated as a security incident, not a routine key-management question, because it usually means either the key was generated by someone with account access who should not have had it, or the account's credentials were compromised in some other way first.

The immediate self-service step available to any admin is revoking the specific key from Settings → Developer → API keys, which takes effect immediately and stops any further use of it. Determining how the key came to exist and what data it accessed while active is a security review a human carries out, using the account's own request logs.

Reporting it to support alongside revoking the key gets that investigation started, and support can also flag or restrict the account further while the review is underway if the situation warrants it.

title: Investigating an unrecognised sign-in
body:
A pattern of failed two-factor attempts followed by an unrecognised successful sign-in is reviewed as a security matter — determining what was accessed during that session requires a human reviewer to examine the account's actual activity log for that session, which is not exposed in a form the account holder can just read off a settings page themselves.

The account owner should change their password and, if possible, reset two-factor enrolment immediately, which invalidates the compromised session going forward, and then contact support to request the activity review for what happened during the session itself.

Because what was accessed differs completely from one incident to the next, this is investigated case by case rather than described generically, and the outcome is communicated directly to the account owner once the review is complete.

title: Reporting an unrecognised admin added to a workspace
body:
A new admin-level user appearing on a workspace with nobody able to account for the invite is treated as a potential compromise, since admin access is the highest level of control a workspace has and an unrecognised addition at that level warrants review before assuming it was a simple mistake.

An existing admin can remove the unrecognised user immediately from Settings → People, which is a reasonable first step regardless of cause, but reporting it to support alongside that removal is what gets a review of how the user came to be added — whether through a compromised admin account, a misused invite link, or something else — since that determines whether anything else needs to be locked down.

This kind of review examines the account's own invite and access history and is handled case by case by a human reviewer.

title: Reporting an unrecognised change to SSO configuration
body:
An SSO configuration pointing at an identity provider domain the workspace does not recognise is treated as a potential compromise of an admin-level setting, since changing where sign-in redirects to is exactly the kind of change an attacker with admin access would make to intercept future logins.

An admin who still has access can revert the SSO configuration to disable it or point it back at the correct provider from Settings → Security → SSO, which stops staff being redirected further, but should also report the change to support so a reviewer can examine when and how the setting was changed and by which account.

Because staff may have already been redirected through the unfamiliar domain before the change was caught, the review also looks at whether any credentials may have been exposed during that window, which is handled case by case rather than assumed either way.

title: Reporting a webhook endpoint that was changed without authorisation
body:
A webhook endpoint repointed to a domain the account does not control means customer data has genuinely been delivered somewhere outside the workspace's own systems for as long as it was in effect, which makes this a security incident rather than a configuration question.

An admin can disable or repoint the webhook immediately from Settings → Developer → Webhooks, which stops further deliveries right away, but should also report it to support so a reviewer can determine when the endpoint was changed, by which account, and what data was delivered to the unauthorised domain during that window.

Because the scope of what was exposed depends entirely on what the webhook was configured to send and for how long, this is investigated case by case against the account's own delivery log rather than something a general article can size in advance.

title: Reclaiming admin access when the sole admin has left the company
body:
A workspace with a single admin account who has left the company and was never offboarded needs its ownership transferred through a verification process, rather than through self-service, because Meridian has no way to know from the account alone that the person requesting the change now represents the company and the former employee does not.

Support handles this by verifying the requester's authority to act for the company — typically through a combination of company email domain, a role on record, and supporting documentation — before granting admin access on the workspace, since granting it to the wrong party would hand control of the account to someone with no real claim to it.

Because what counts as sufficient proof varies by situation, this is reviewed case by case by a human, and the process is initiated by contacting support directly rather than through any in-product flow.

title: Transferring workspace ownership
body:
Ownership of a workspace can be transferred to a new point of contact, but because it is a change of who has ultimate control over the account, it is handled by a human reviewer rather than a self-service setting, even when the change is entirely legitimate and uncontested.

The reviewer verifies the new contact's standing to request the transfer — generally confirming they are acting for the same company that owns the account — before completing it, which protects against a transfer being requested by someone outside the company with no real claim to it.

Requests are reviewed case by case since what is available to confirm identity varies by situation, and a transfer is initiated by contacting support with the new contact's details.

title: Regaining access after losing both recovery email and two-factor device
body:
Losing access to both the recovery email and the two-factor device on the only admin account removes every self-service recovery path at once, which is why this specific combination is handled through a manual identity verification with support rather than an automated reset.

A reviewer works through alternative ways to confirm the requester is the legitimate account owner — this can include company domain ownership, billing history details only the account owner would know, or other account-specific verification — since none of the usual automated resets apply when both factors are gone.

Because the exact verification path depends on what is available for a given account, this is handled case by case, and the account owner should contact support directly rather than attempt repeated recovery attempts through the normal sign-in flow.

title: Handling a dispute over who owns a workspace
body:
When two people from the same company each claim to be the rightful owner of a workspace and are asking for the other's access to be revoked, Meridian does not take either side's word for it — a support reviewer treats this as an internal company matter that needs to be resolved on the company's side, with documentation, before any access change is made.

This typically means the review is paused pending some form of confirmation from the company itself — such as a statement from someone in a position of authority over both parties — rather than Meridian arbitrating the dispute directly, since Meridian has no way to independently judge an internal disagreement.

Because every situation like this differs, it is handled case by case by a human reviewer, and either party can start the process by contacting support with their account details.

title: Transferring ownership after an acquisition
body:
An acquisition changing who should control a workspace is one of the more involved ownership transfers Meridian handles, since it requires establishing that the acquisition is genuine before any access changes, and that kind of verification is not something an in-product flow can do on its own.

A reviewer typically asks for documentation establishing the acquisition — this can include public announcements, legal documentation, or confirmation from a contact at the acquired company — and coordinates the transfer once satisfied, rather than acting on the acquiring company's assertion alone.

Because acquisitions vary widely in how they are structured and documented, this is reviewed case by case, and the process starts with the acquiring company's representative contacting support directly.

title: Updating the email tied to your account after it no longer exists
body:
An account whose registered email address no longer exists — for example, after leaving a previous employer — cannot receive the usual email-based verification a routine email change would use, which means confirming the request is genuinely coming from the account owner needs a different path.

Support verifies the requester's identity through alternative means, which can include billing history, account-specific details, or other confirmation not dependent on the old email address, before updating the account's registered email to a new one.

Because what is available to verify identity depends on the specific account, this is reviewed case by case by a human reviewer, and the account owner should contact support directly rather than attempt a standard password or email reset, which would still route through the address that no longer exists.

title: Restoring access after a suspension for a failed payment
body:
A workspace suspended after a card on file expired and a renewal charge failed is reviewed once a new payment method is added, rather than restored automatically the instant a new card is entered, because the billing team confirms the new charge actually succeeds before lifting a suspension.

Adding a new card is self-service from Settings → Billing → Payment method, but the retry of the failed charge and the resulting restoration of access is processed by the billing team, generally within a short window after the new card is added rather than instantly, since a charge attempt itself can take a moment to confirm.

Because suspension and restoration touch active billing state, the exact timing for a given account is confirmed by the billing team rather than promised in advance by a general article.

title: Tracing a bank transfer payment that hasn't been applied
body:
A bank transfer that has cleared on the paying company's side but has not yet been applied to the account's balance is investigated by the billing team, since applying it correctly means matching the incoming transfer to the right account and invoice, which is not something the account owner can do from their own settings.

Bank transfers can take longer to reconcile than a card charge because they arrive through a separate banking channel from the one Meridian's billing system watches automatically, and matching one to an account sometimes requires details only the paying company has, such as the exact reference used on the transfer.

Providing the transfer date, amount and reference to the billing team is what lets them trace it against incoming transfers and apply it to the account; this is handled case by case since matching details vary per payment.

title: Removing a payment method after a lost card
body:
A payment method can be removed from Settings → Billing → Payment method, provided it is not the only method on file for an account with an active subscription — a workspace needs at least one valid payment method able to be charged.

Whether every trace of a removed card is fully gone from the billing system, and not just hidden from the settings page, is a question the billing team confirms directly rather than something the settings page itself asserts — this matters specifically after a lost-card incident, where the concern is about the card being usable elsewhere rather than just unlisted here.

Because this involves confirming the state of the account's billing record rather than just its visible settings, it is handled case by case by the billing team on request, and the account owner or billing contact should raise it after removing the method themselves.

title: What happens after a chargeback
body:
A chargeback reverses a payment at the bank level, outside of Meridian's own systems, and Meridian's billing team is notified of it separately from the account simply continuing to run — the account is not automatically suspended the moment a chargeback is filed, since chargebacks are themselves disputed and resolved through the card network's own process.

The billing team reviews the chargeback and generally reaches out to the account's billing contact about it, since a chargeback affects the account's standing and next steps once the card network's process resolves it.

A customer who wants to settle the underlying balance directly, separately from how the chargeback itself resolves, should contact the billing team rather than assume the two will reconcile on their own, since a chargeback and a direct settlement are handled through different processes.

title: Confirming a change from card to invoiced billing
body:
Moving from automatic card billing to invoiced bank payment is arranged with the billing team rather than changed directly in self-service settings, since invoiced billing is a different billing arrangement with its own payment terms rather than just a different payment method on the same automatic setup.

Once set up, the billing team can confirm the new arrangement is in place and will apply to the next invoice, which is a reasonable thing to ask for in writing before a large invoice goes out, especially where a customer wants certainty before the switch takes effect rather than finding out after the invoice is generated.

Because invoiced billing terms can vary by account, confirming the specific details for a given account is something the billing team provides directly rather than a general article can state.

title: Getting written confirmation before a payment method change
body:
A finance team wanting confirmation of the exact amount and date of an upcoming charge before authorising a payment method change is a reasonable request the billing team can fulfil directly, since the amount depends on the account's current plan, seats and any pending overages, and the date depends on the account's specific billing cycle — neither of which a general article can state for every account.

The billing team can provide this confirmation in writing ahead of the change, which is worth requesting explicitly rather than assuming the dashboard's summary figures are final, since a summary shown before a change does not always reflect proration or timing precisely enough for a formal authorisation.

Because this involves account-specific figures, it is handled case by case by the billing team on request, generally with enough lead time to review before the charge date in question.

title: Recognising fraudulent billing emails
body:
Meridian never asks a customer to wire funds to a bank account communicated by email, and never asks for payment outside of the payment methods configured directly in the account's own billing settings — a request to wire money to a new account, especially one presented as urgent or overdue, does not match how Meridian actually collects payment.

Any customer unsure whether a billing email is genuine should not act on it directly — no reply, no click on a link in it, and no payment — and should instead check their account's actual billing status from Settings → Billing, comparing what it shows against what the email claims.

Forwarding a suspicious email to support lets it be confirmed as fraudulent and, where useful, flagged so other customers who may have received the same message can be warned.

title: Two-factor codes are never requested by phone or support
body:
Meridian support never asks a customer to read out a two-factor authentication code over the phone, by chat, or by any channel — a code is only ever entered directly into Meridian's own sign-in page by the account holder, and a request to say it aloud or type it anywhere else is a strong signal of an attempt to take over the account rather than a legitimate identity check.

Legitimate identity verification with support does not involve the two-factor code at all; it uses other account details instead, precisely because the code exists to prove a sign-in is happening on the real site and handing it to someone else defeats that purpose entirely.

Anyone who received this kind of call should not provide the code, should end the call, and should report it to support so the account can be checked for any related unauthorised activity.

title: Verifying a suspicious invoice
body:
Every genuine invoice Meridian generates is also available from Settings → Billing → Invoices inside the account itself, so an invoice received by email that does not match anything shown there is worth treating as unverified until confirmed, rather than paid on the strength of the email alone.

Genuine invoices reflect the account's actual plan, seats and usage for a real billing period; an invoice referencing an amount or due date with no corresponding entry in the account's own billing history is a mismatch worth investigating before any payment is made against it.

Forwarding the email to support allows it to be checked against the account's real billing record and confirmed as genuine or flagged as fraudulent.

title: Recognising executive-impersonation requests about payment details
body:
A message that impersonates an executive and asks an employee to urgently change payment details is a common fraud pattern, and referencing real, correct account details in the message does not make the request more legitimate — that information is often available to an attacker from public sources or a prior compromise elsewhere, not proof they are who they claim to be.

Payment method changes for an account go through Meridian's own billing settings or the billing team directly, verified against the account, never through an unverified message asking an employee to act urgently outside of that process, regardless of who the message appears to be from.

An employee who receives a request like this should verify it directly with the person it claims to be from, through a channel other than the one the message arrived on, before taking any action, and should report the message to support so the account can be checked for related activity.

title: What an unrequested password-reset email means
body:
A password-reset email that was not requested by the account owner means someone else entered that account's email address into the sign-in page's reset flow — the email itself does not grant access on its own, since it only becomes a working reset link if it is clicked and completed, but it does confirm someone attempted to start that process.

The safest response is not to click the link in an unrequested reset email, and instead to check the account's sign-in and security settings directly, and to change the password proactively as a precaution even though the attempted reset was not completed.

Reporting it to support lets the account's recent access history be checked for anything beyond the reset attempt itself, since a reset attempt is sometimes the first step in a broader attempt rather than an isolated one.

title: What to do after entering credentials on a lookalike sign-in page
body:
A sign-in page that looks like Meridian's but was reached through a link in an unsolicited email, rather than by typing Meridian's own address or using a saved bookmark, should be treated as untrusted regardless of how convincing it looks — checking the address bar for the genuine domain before entering anything is the reliable way to tell the two apart, but that check has to happen before credentials are entered, not after.

If credentials were entered on such a page, they should be treated as exposed: the password should be changed immediately from Meridian's real sign-in page, and two-factor authentication should be reset if it is enabled, since a phishing page can capture whatever is typed into it including a one-time code entered at the same time.

Reporting the incident to support lets the account's recent sign-in activity be checked for any sign the exposed credentials were already used before the password change took effect.
